Our concern is not merely procedural. The MOU, its annexes, and the related governments, administration, and operational arrangement have substantive implication for the governance, institutional character, accountability and functioning of the Cali Fund and the multilateral mechanism. They address inter alia the role and responsibility of the institution involved, decision making and oversight, administration of contribution and disbursement and relationship with the fund and the governance structure established pursuant to decision 16.3. We recall that the multilateral mechanism, including the Cali Fund, was established by the Conference of the Parties through decision 16/2. Arrangement affecting its governance and institutional architecture should therefore remain within the mandate established by the Parties and under the authority and guidance of the Conference of the Parties. Concluding and operationalizing such arrangement before Parties have an opportunity to consider them raise important concern regarding the transparency, accountability and the perceived role. We are particularly concerned that the arrangement could affect the fundamental collectors of the Cali Fund. The fund was established as a part of the multilateral mechanism for the fair and equitable sharing of benefit arising from the use of the digital sequence information on genetic resource. It should therefore remain a benefit sharing fund and shouldn't, through its governance, financing or operational arrangement, evolve into conventional dollar driving fund. Confidence in the Cali Fund is not only about whether companies and other entities trust the fund sufficiently to contribute. The confidence of the party in its governance, legitimacy, benefit sharing character is equally essential. Parties must have confidence that the contribution to the fund constitute genuine benefit sharing under the multilateral mechanism and that its governance remain consistent with decision 16.2 and the collective decision of the COP. There is also direct relevance to the Cali Fund certificate. Their credibility and practical value depend on the confidence that the contributions they represent are made to legitimate benefit sharing mechanism. If the fund is perceived as a donor driven fund rather than a benefit sharing mechanism, parties may question the recognition, legal effect or regulatory relevance of such certificate under the national measures. This could weaken the value of the contribution entity of the contributing entity and ultimately undermine confidence in the multilateral mechanism itself. For this reason, arrangement already concluded or operationalized through shouldn't be treated as a fake accomplice. We would call the memorandum understanding its annex and all related governance and administrative and operational document and arrangement including those developed or adopted by the steering committee and those concerning the Cali Fund certification to be submitted to the Conference of the Parties for its consideration and review without prejudice to the view of the parties on their content and status. The COP should review this arrangement for their consistency and alignment with decision 16/2 and where necessary provide for the amendment to preserve the benefit sharing character of the Cali Fund, ensuring transparency and accountability, safeguarding the authority and guidance of the COP. and provide a credible basis for the recognition of the Cali certificate. We believe that acknowledging and correcting such concern rather than allowing contested arrangement to become established practice, it is essential to restoring and maintaining party confidence in the Cali fund and the effectiveness of the multilateral mechanism would depend not only on attracting contribution but also in its legitimacy, credibility and party driven governance.
